components.name: cookie-name
components.description: An HTTP token chosen by the application; the standard assigns no meaning to any name.

components.name: cookie-value
components.description: Zero or more cookie-octets (no whitespace, double quote, comma, semicolon or backslash), optionally in double quotes; for a session identifier cookie it is the nonce and is the credential span.

components.name: cookie-attributes
components.description: Set-Cookie attributes (Expires, Max-Age, Domain, Path, Secure, HttpOnly); they describe the scope and handling of the cookie, are not returned in a Cookie header and are outside the credential span.

claims.statement: A request Cookie header carries cookie-pairs separated by "; "; a Set-Cookie header carries one cookie-pair followed by attribute-value pairs. A cookie-value has no whitespace, double quote, comma, semicolon or backslash and may be empty.

sources.supports: cookie-header = "Cookie:" OWS cookie-string OWS; cookie-string = cookie-pair *( ";" SP cookie-pair ); cookie-value = *cookie-octet / ( DQUOTE *cookie-octet DQUOTE )

claims.statement: The semantics of a cookie name and value are not defined by the standard; servers give each cookie application-specific meaning, so a name alone does not establish that a cookie is an authentication secret.

sources.supports: The semantics of the cookie-value are not defined by this document
The semantics of individual cookies in the Cookie header are not defined by this document. Servers are expected to imbue these cookies with application-specific semantics

claims.statement: A session identifier stored in a cookie is a nonce the server uses to look up session state; anyone who learns or replays it can interact with the server with the session's authority, and a cookie is a form of ambient authority.

sources.supports: servers commonly store a nonce (or "session identifier") in a cookie ... the nonce is useful only for interacting with the server
cookies being a form of ambient authority

claims.statement: Cookie content that is not a nonce may itself be sensitive, so absence of a session-identifier role does not by itself make a cookie value harmless.

sources.supports: using session identifier cookies limits the damage ... (unlike non-nonce cookie content, which might itself be sensitive)

claims.statement: Cookie attributes (Domain, Path, Secure, HttpOnly, Expires, Max-Age) define scope and handling; they are not returned in the Cookie header, so a server cannot tell from the header alone how a cookie was set.

sources.supports: the cookie attributes are not returned ... the server cannot determine from the Cookie header alone when a cookie will expire, for which hosts or paths the cookie is valid, or whether the cookie was set with the Secure or HttpOnly attributes

claims.statement: Several Set-Cookie header lines are never folded into one comma-joined field, because a comma is used inside Set-Cookie values; Cookie carries many pairs in one line.

sources.supports: Origin servers SHOULD NOT fold multiple Set-Cookie header fields into a single header field
Set-Cookie ... cannot be combined into a single field value, recipients ought to handle Set-Cookie as a special case

claims.statement: HTTP itself notes that custom user-authentication mechanisms pass authentication tokens in Cookie and Set-Cookie.

sources.supports: various custom mechanisms for user authentication use the Set-Cookie and Cookie header fields for passing tokens related to authentication

claims.statement: A third-party guide lists framework default session cookie names (for example PHPSESSID, JSESSIONID, ASP.NET_SessionId) and says an established session ID is temporarily equivalent to the strongest authentication method used; this is a lead, not a rule that a given name is a session cookie.

sources.supports: the session ID (or token) is temporarily equivalent to the strongest authentication method used by the application; session ID names used by common frameworks can be fingerprinted, such as PHPSESSID, JSESSIONID, ASP.NET_SessionId

claims.statement: No source states which cookie names or value shapes mark a session identifier versus an ordinary preference or tracking cookie.

sources.supports: The semantics of the cookie-value are not defined by this document

notes: Project-authored by the Redact Secret project, which maintains this repository; not independent evidence. Draft; not yet reviewed.

openQuestions.question: Which cookie names or contexts establish a session-identifier role without application knowledge? Product recognition policy is handed off.

Should ordinary preference, consent and opaque application-state cookies be expected unflagged? The standard says non-nonce content might itself be sensitive, so the outcome stays a maintainer decision.
RFC 6265 was read as published in 2011; whether a successor revision changes the cookie grammar was not established in this review.
